query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The oxidation resistance and material integrity of multiprincipal-element alloys in harsh high-temperature environments are governed by the formation of a protective oxide layer, which is influenced by the alloy composition and environmental conditions.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of alloy composition and environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, oxygen partial pressure)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3, SiO2)
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic and kinetic processes controlling the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxidation resistance and material integrity with optimized alloy composition and environmental conditions
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory alloys with poor oxidation resistance
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 1000 °C - 1300 °C; Oxygen partial pressure range: 10^-14 - 1 atm
generation.uncertainty: Limited understanding of the complex interdependence between alloy chemistry, mechanical behavior, and thermodynamic stability

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with systematic variation of alloy composition and environmental conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation resistance and material integrity of the multiprincipal-element alloys do not improve with optimized alloy composition and environmental conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications (e.g. fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions.Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations Refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have recently been developed in the context of high-temperature and severe environmental applications. In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

The so-called high-entropy alloys based on the refractory elements (refractory high-entropy alloys, RHEAs) are considered as candidates for high-temperature applications [,,,,]. Some of them have high strength at T ≥ 1000 °C and thus can potentially operate at higher temperatures than commercial nickel-based superalloys [,,,,,,,,,]. Some RHEAs are sufficiently ductile at room temperature even in tension [,,,,] and can be cold rolled [,,,]. However, refractory elements and their alloys are generally vulnerable to oxidation. A number of studies focused on oxidation behavior of different RHEAs [,,,,,,,,,,] have demonstrated that some of them possess much better oxidation resistance than conventional refractory alloys; however, the oxidation behavior strongly depended on the alloy composition and testing conditions. Note that the vast majority of the performed research was conducted at temperatures of T ≥ 1000 °C [,,,,,,].

Titanium achieves its excellent corrosion protection because of the high stability of the passive layer that develops on its surface [], which can be re-formed at body temperature and in physiological fluid if it is damaged. The increased popularity of Ti and its alloys as important biomaterials is driven by their low modulus [,,], greater biocompatibility, and better corrosion resistance in comparison to traditional biomaterials, such as stainless steel and Co–Cr alloys []. These desirable qualities were the motivating force for the early insertion of Ti as an implantable material. Ti has low mechanical strength [,], and when aluminum and vanadium are incorporated in low amounts, the resistance of the alloy is greatly improved over that of titanium and the alloy could be successfully used in severe stress situations, such as Ti–6Al–4V, which has been predominantly employed. However, Ti–6Al–4V has significant toxicity; harmful tissue reactions are caused by vanadium and the release of both V and Al ions are related to long-term health disorders such as peripheral neuropathy and Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases [,].
